Facial Expressions

How the games in your library do faces, and one expression set our characters can use. Pick a feeling: the 3D toy, its painted 2D twin and the faceless mannequin all play it from the same numbers. Then type a line, and the line drives the face.

Drag to orbit, pinch to zoom. When the face gets smaller than about 40 pixels it stops reading, so the character pushes its expression and body harder and a little bubble appears over its head. The bubble is only drawn for you; nobody in the world can see it.

Say a line

Tags in square brackets set the feeling from that word on, and the voice gets the same tags. Without tags, a question mark makes the face curious and "..." makes it think. The mouth shapes come from the letters.

How the voice and the line drive it

One line, written once, drives the voice and the face. Scripted lines are rendered ahead with timestamps, so the mouth is exact; live lines stream, and the face follows word timings or simply the loudness.

  • Scripted lines (the school jump, the basement): render ahead with the cast voice and its timestamps, store the visemes next to the audio, play them in lockstep. Exact, and free at play time.
  • Live lines (the characters answering Abbie): stream the same voice; the face follows word timings when the voice sends them, otherwise the loudness opens the jaw. The feeling still comes from the line's tags.
  • The game drives it too: like the kerbals, a feeling can come from what happens (a coin found, the dog barking), not just from a script. The mood under it is what the character feels all scene.

Rules for Abbie's World

  • Kids' faces are never redrawn. The kit only moves the parts a character already has (lids, brows, mouth). It never paints or generates a likeness, and never uses a photo. Family characters keep the faces on their approved sheets.
  • PG always. Grumpy, not furious; worried, not terrified; "yuck", not gross-out. No blood, no horror faces, no mocking.
  • No player-face capture. Before Your Eyes reads your blinks by webcam; we keep a kid's camera off.
  • Face is world, bubble is presentation. The face and body are part of the character, so other characters can react to them. The far-away bubble is drawn only for the player.
  • Camera first, then the face budget. Close camera: eyes and brows matter most. Iso or far: push the body and summon a bubble or a portrait (Hades) instead of shrinking the face.
  • Eyes alive or not at all. Blinks, eye darts and a held beat after each line; otherwise go faceless or painted (the Andromeda lesson).

  • Put the face rig on the rigged wooden mannequin and the Meshy heroes from the character studio (AW-STUDY-0037), and the 18 feelings into the 2D puppet as one-tap stock expressions.
  • Render the family cast's scripted lines with timestamps and store the visemes beside the audio.
  • One art-direction pass per style: claymation (big brows, squashy mouth), stick figure (swap sheet), 1980s action cartoon (hard brows, held poses), comic hero (Marvel Rivals style shading on the same rig).
